justification: run-code is green and reproduced 3x with identical block/executed counts and no flakiness. I independently re-ran every EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN scenario myself in a standalone node:sqlite script (SQLite 3.50.4, same engine family as the article's node:sqlite) rather than trusting run-code.mjs alone: full scan → SCAN hit; single-column index → SEARCH ... USING INDEX; composite (visitor_id, hit_at) satisfies a query on both columns but a query on hit_at alone falls back to SCAN; swapped order (hit_at, visitor_id) flips which query gets SEARCH vs SCAN; a covering index produces the literal string 'SEARCH hit USING COVERING INDEX idx_cover (visitor_id=?)' when the select list is covered, and drops to plain 'USING INDEX' when it is not; a case-insensitive LIKE pattern against a BINARY-collated index scans, and re-indexing with COLLATE NOCASE turns it into a SEARCH range scan; substr(hit_at,1,7) on an indexed hit_at column also scans. Every one of my reproductions matched the article's shown output verbatim, including the internal 'notused' integers (61, 62, 55, 165, 216) and page counts, which is strong evidence the transcripts are real captures and not typed-up approximations. I also fetched and read fileformat2.html, queryplanner.html, eqp.html, optoverview.html, expridx.html and the Microsoft Learn overview myself and checked every quoted sentence word-for-word against the live pages: the b-tree/leaf/interior definitions, the four EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN fields, the SCAN/SEARCH definitions, the rowid-binary-search-then-table-binary-search description, the 'still much faster than doing a full table scan' line, the (fruit, state) 'simply ignoring the state column' example, the prefix-index rule of thumb, the covering-index paragraph ('saves one binary search for each row'), the case_sensitive_like/BINARY/NOCASE pairing (verified character-for-character), the 'query planner does not do algebra' line, and the Microsoft Learn 'lightweight ADO.NET provider for SQLite' phrase — all are accurate, in-context, and support the sentence they're attached to. Both self-caught misattributions the writer reported are genuinely fixed in the final text, and I found the mechanism by which they'd have been wrong: queryplanner.html's 'N/logN, about 1 million times faster' line lives in the ROWID-lookup section (1.2), not the secondary-index section (1.3) — the article correctly cites the 1.3 sentence instead for its visitor_id (non-key) lookup, and the '1 million' figure and 'N/logN' phrase appear nowhere on the page. The (fruit, state) example is SQLite's own worked example, quoted accurately, with no invented (state, city) substitute anywhere in the text. The dbstat page-count interpretation is correct and I re-derived the same conclusion: root (1 page, 5 keys/6 pointers) → 6 interior pages (397-442 cells each) → 2,518 leaves is a 3-level tree, so 3 page reads reach any row, and the exercise's 10x-growth argument (root stays under capacity, at most one more interior level, 3→4 page reads vs. a full scan's 10x) is sound, appropriately expressed as an upper bound rather than an exact prediction. The write-cost measurement (0 vs 3 indexes, 50,000 inserts) is methodologically sound — one transaction, a reused parameterized command, min-of-4-batches — and the stated overhead range ('roughly a quarter to two-thirds more time') brackets the actual ratios implied by the stated ms ranges (98/80≈1.22, 105/66≈1.59). The seek/scan ratio claim ('roughly two thousand to five thousand times faster') likewise brackets the ratio implied by the article's own stated ms ranges (7.6/0.0037≈2054 to 7.8/0.0014≈5571), and the piece explicitly and correctly flags sub-microsecond timings as noise rather than overclaiming precision. The dual-SQLite-version disclosure (3.50 for sql run/dbstat/EQP blocks vs. 3.41.2, self-reported and printed by the program, for the three csharp timing blocks) is present, explicit, and honestly hedged ('need not match the 3.50 running the blocks above'); crucially it creates no inconsistency because the csharp blocks never print an EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN or any query-plan-shaped claim — they only time queries and print sqlite_version(), so there is no place on the page where the two versions' plan wording could visibly disagree. The 'sqlite_version: 3.41.2' line is not wildcarded in the output block, meaning run-code.mjs's exact-match comparison genuinely verified that literal string against a live run, not a claim taken on faith. The toolchain statement is correctly placed beside the first real measurement (the scan-timing block), not the opening paragraph, satisfying the editorial brief's placement rule, and the article states the SQLite-3.50-session fact separately, at its own first use, rather than stamping both facts at the top. Against comparison sources: Use The Index, Luke's own B-tree anatomy chapter and PostgreSQL's indexes-intro chapter are both explicitly conceptual, with no real EXPLAIN output and no concrete measurements (Use The Index, Luke defers detail to later chapters; PostgreSQL defers performance analysis to its own Chapter 14). This article's EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN- and dbstat-driven treatment, with every plan reproducible and every number machine-verified, is genuinely more concrete and falsifiable than either, and covers a wider and more concrete set of cases (column-order sensitivity, covering indexes, two distinct index-defeat mechanisms, a real write-cost measurement) than either source attempts in one place. I found no factual error that would cap the score at 7. Two minor issues keep it from a higher score: one front-matter source (lang_createindex.html) is never cited inline, and 'the hidden rowid that backs hit_id' slightly misdescribes SQLite's rowid aliasing (an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY column IS the rowid, per lang_createtable.html's 'the column becomes an alias for the rowid', not a separate hidden column that a visible one is 'backed by') — a terminology nit that does not affect any of the load-bearing claims (the table b-tree genuinely is keyed by rowid/hit_id's value, and every subsequent depth/page-count argument is unaffected).

issues.location: Section 'What SQLite actually walks', first sentence: "keyed by the hidden rowid that backs hit_id"
issues.problem: Slightly misdescribes SQLite's rowid aliasing. `hit_id` is declared `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` (exact type name "INTEGER"), so per SQLite's own CREATE TABLE documentation it "becomes an alias for the rowid" — there is no separate hidden rowid column that hit_id is backed by; hit_id's stored value and the rowid are the same thing under two names. The phrase as written implies a two-column relationship (a hidden backing field plus a visible hit_id field) that doesn't exist here. This doesn't affect the B-tree/depth arguments that follow, which remain correct either way.
issues.fixLooksLike: "...keyed by the rowid, which hit_id aliases (per SQLite's rules for an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY column)" or similar, citing lang_createtable.html's alias language instead of implying a hidden backing column.
